lawyer:
Mr. Miah Abdul Gofur, Advocate ----- for the appellant.
Mr. Fakir Abdul Mannan with Mr. M.G. Bhuiyan, Advocates ----- for the respondent.
full_judgment: 12. The learned Advocate for the appellant next contended that the defendant was in doubt as to whom he is to pay the rent and as such he was not a defaulter. Section 19(2) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance speaks that in the case of bonafide doubt or dispute as to the person who is entitled to the rent, the tenant is to make deposit to the House Rent Controller. But in the present case no deposit was made and the tenant is undoubtedly a defaulter under the law. Mr. Gafur argued that the tenant thought that he is not to pay rent to the plaintiff as the property is a vested property The tenant went into possession under an agreement of tenancy and he is guided by the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and if there is a bonafide doubt the is to deposit cate appearing for the respondent has rightly pointed out that the case of fraud or misrepresentation having not been at all made out and the admitted position being that the defendant is a tenant he is precluded to challenge the title of the landlord. The learned Advocate for the respondent placed before us the deed of agreement Exhibit 'A' and the tenancy is determined by this agreement where the plaintiff asserted that he is absolute ownerin the suit holding and the defendant accepted the same and proposed to occupy the same premises on payment of the rent. In such circumstances, we agree with the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the defendant is precluded to question the title of the plaintiff. Let us now take up the decision cited by the learned Advocate on this point. Mr. Gafur cited a case reported in A.I.R. 1928 Bombay 265. In that reported decision it has been held that if once the relationship of landlord and tenant is established between the parties, the tenant is precluded from disputing the title of the landlord. The reported decision was a case where the tenant was in possession before the new tenancy began and he executed a lease of tenancy which constituted a new tenancy and allotment . So in that case the question was whether a new tenancy had arises or not, whether the tenant had been let into possession by the landlord. Thus, this decision has got no manner of application in the facts of the present case. In that reported decision the tenant asserted that the contract of tenancy is void or vioidable on account of misrepresentation or fraud. In that decision the decree of the trial court was uphold for recovery of rent even by holding that if the tenant contends that the land does not belong to the plaintiff and title lies somewhere, it is open to him to surrender the possession and to establish his title in a different suit. We fail to understand who the decision is applicable in the facts of the present case. The next case cited is A.I.R. 1926 Calcutta that was a case where through ignorance landlord or by fraud in the matter of execution of the kabuliyat the tenants adorned the landlord and the tenants are not altogether estopped but can show that the land-lord had no title either when the kabuliyat was executed or attotnment was made by payment of rent. In the reported decision the tenants were also in possession of the holding from before whereas in the present case with which we were dealing the tenant was inducted by the landlord and the present case is not a case of attornment and the tenant was inducted into possession by the plaintiff. Thus, we fail to understand how Mr. Gafur can cite such a case which is not relevant for the present decision. In A.I.R. 1956 Calcutta 148 it has been clearly held that the estoppel under section 116 of the Evidence Act is confined to the time when the tenancy commenced and the reported case was a money suit for compensation only for use and occupation. Further in that decision it was held that the suit was one purely for money and not a suit for recovery of possession of immovable property as such this decision is also of no help to the learned Advocate for the appellant. Mr. Gafur also cited the case reported in XXXIII D.L.R. (AD) 37, which was a case of attornment; means the act of the tenant putting one person in place of another as his landlord. It was further held in that decision that in the case of attornment the tenant may not be estopped and the Rule is not infleible. Thus reading of this decision we are of the view that this being a case of attornment of subsequent landlord under a mistaken fact has no manner of application to the fact the appellant cited a case reported in XXIV D.L.R. 202. In that reported decision the plaintiff Dr. Rati Ranjan Chowdhury filed a suit for ejectment against defendant No. 1 Parul Bala Marwari and defendant No. 2 Md. Ibrahim. Defendant No. 2 as her sub-tenant in the holding stated that after the death of her husband she inducted defendant No. 2 . In the written statement defendant No. 2 denied the title of the plaintiff. Thus, the court found that there is no nexus between the plaintiff and the rent before the House Rent Controller. But the tenant cannot take the plea that he is not to deposit the rent anywhere and continue to remain in possession for such a long time without payment of rent to anybody. The learned Subordinate Judge has correctly held that the defendant should at least deposit the rent before the House Rent Controller under section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. The tenant having not done so is to be held to be a defaulter in the eye of law. When we put the question to Mr. Gafur the learned Advocate for the appellant as to why the rent was not deposited he submitted that the defendant was under the impression that the custodian is the proper authority for obtaining the money. This is a flimsy argument and the argument was untenable because of the simple fact that no money was also paid to House Rent Controller for protection of his tenancy. The learned Subordinate Judge has rightly rejected this point. Mr. Gafur further submitted that under section 36 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance the defendant is not to pay the rent to the plaintiff. We fail to understand how such an argument can be advanced by the learned Advocate for the appellant when there is nothing on record to show that the suit holding in question is owned by the Government and there is no iota of evidence that the custodian ever claimed the property as such. Thus this point is also of no substance.
